problem.summary: Standard detectors predict a fixed set of pre-defined categories learned from crowd-labeled data that is costly to scale and covers at most a couple thousand concepts, so models need new labeled data for every new concept or domain and cannot generalize zero-shot.
statements: Detection models trained on a fixed category set require additional labeled data to generalize to new visual concepts and domains.
Human-annotated detection annotations are expensive to scale, and even the largest detection datasets cover no more than about 2,000 categories.
Self-training with a fixed-vocabulary detector teacher cannot introduce concepts outside the teacher's label pool.
Image-level pre-training (CLIP) gives semantic but not fine-grained object-level representations needed for detection-style tasks.

evidence.quote: Visual recognition models are typically trained to predict a fixed set of pre-determined object categories, which limits their usability in real-world applications since additional labeled data are needed to generalize to new visual concepts and domains.
However, human annotations have been proven costy and limited [15, 30].
The largest attempts at scaling up detection vocabulary still cover no more than 2,000 categories [15, 28].

background.summary: GLIP builds on CLIP/ALIGN-style image-text contrastive pre-training, on DyHead as the detection backbone/head, on MDETR's grounding formulation, and on prior zero-shot/open-vocabulary detectors (ViLD), claiming the gap is that no prior method unifies detection and grounding to use both detection and grounding data plus web-scale image-text pairs.

relatedWork.name: CLIP
relatedWork.relation: image-level vision-language pre-training that is semantic but not object-level
relatedWork.quote: CLIP [45] shows that image-level visual representations can be learned effectively on large amounts of raw image-text pairs.

relatedWork.name: DyHead
relatedWork.relation: the SoTA detector used as GLIP's image encoder; reformulated to show equivalence
relatedWork.quote: Though our current implementation is built upon Dynamic Head (DyHead) [10], our unified formulation can be generalized to any object detection systems

relatedWork.name: MDETR
relatedWork.relation: prior phrase-grounding model whose fine-grained contrastive loss inspired the grounding loss
relatedWork.quote: Our grounding formulation is inspired by MDETR [23], and our grounding loss shares the same spirit of MDETR's fine-grained contrastive loss.

relatedWork.name: ViLD
relatedWork.relation: zero-shot detection by distilling CLIP/ALIGN into a two-stage detector
relatedWork.quote: By distilling the knowledge from the CLIP/ALIGN model into a two-stage detector, ViLD [14] is proposed to advance zero-shot object detection.

evidence.quote: Standard object detection systems are trained to localize a fixed set of object classes predefined in crowd-labeled datasets, such as COCO [37], OpenImages (OI) [30], Objects365 [50], and Visual Genome (VG) [28], which contains no more than 2,000 object classes.

solution.summary: GLIP reformulates object detection as phrase grounding by replacing the box-classifier logits with word-region alignment scores computed from a text prompt listing candidate categories, adds cross-modality deep fusion between the DyHead image encoder and BERT text encoder, and pre-trains on detection plus grounding data enlarged by teacher-generated pseudo boxes for 24M web image-text pairs.
solution.approach: Ground every region against phrases in a text prompt with a unified loss, fuse vision and language deeply across encoder layers, and self-train on detection, gold grounding, and pseudo-labeled image-text data.
components: text prompt of candidate category phrases for detection
word-region alignment scores replacing classification logits
cross-modality multi-head attention deep fusion (DyHead + BERT)
unified loss for detection and grounding
teacher-student self-training with NLP-parsed noun-phrase pseudo boxes
prompt tuning and manual prompt design for transfer

evidence.quote: Instead of classifying each region/box into c classes, we reformulate detection as a grounding task, by grounding/aligning each region to c phrases in a text prompt (see Figure 2).
Any object detection model can be converted to a grounding model by replacing the object classification logits in its box classifier with the word-region alignment scores

we show that deep cross-modality fusion applied by GLIP, as shown in Figure 2 (Middle), is crucial to learn high-quality language-aware visual representations and to achieve superior transfer learning performance.

We first pre-train a teacher GLIP with gold (human-annotated) detection and grounding data. Then we use this teacher model to predict boxes for web-collected image-text data, with noun phrases detected by an NLP parser [2].

experiments.summary: GLIP is pre-trained on 27M grounding examples (3M human-annotated + 24M web image-text pairs) and evaluated by direct zero-shot transfer on COCO, LVIS and Flickr30K, by full fine-tuning on COCO, and by the 13-dataset ODinW few-shot benchmark with data-efficiency and prompt-tuning ablations.

evidence.quote: GLIP achieves 49.8 AP and 26.9 AP, respectively, surpassing many supervised baselines.
After fine-tuned on COCO, GLIP achieves 60.8 AP on val and 61.5 AP on test-dev, surpassing prior SoTA.
GLIP-L surpasses the current SoTA on COCO, reaching 60.8 on 2017val and 61.5 on test-dev, without some bells and whistles in prior SoTA [65] such as model EMA, mixup, label smoothing, or soft-NMS.
A zero-shot GLIP-T outperforms 5-shot DyHead-T while a one-shot GLIP-L is competitive with a fully supervised DyHead-T.

limitations.summary: The paper has no dedicated limitations section, but the authors note that long category lists cannot fit in one prompt, that deep fusion can hurt novel-category performance when only detection data is used, that models overfit on LVIS/Flickr30K during pre-training, and that the scaling behaviour with image-text data size is not studied.
items: Text prompts are limited to 256 tokens, so large-vocabulary datasets must be split into multiple prompts (minor performance drop).
With only detection data, deep fusion can degrade performance on novel categories because the language model overfits to the pre-training vocabulary.
Models tend to overfit on LVIS and Flickr30K during pre-training, so best checkpoints are selected on validation splits.
A systematic study of scaling with text-image data size is deferred.

evidence.quote: Thus, for certain datasets with a large vocabulary (e.g., Objects365 [50] has 365 object categories), we cannot fit all category names into one prompt.
when grounding data are present, deep fusion degrades common category performance but improves rare category performance
We find that models tend to overfit on LVIS during the course of pre-training so we monitor the performance on minival for all models and report the results with the best checkpoints.
We leave a detailed study of how GLIP scales with text-image data size to future work.

futureDirections.direction: Study how GLIP scales with the size of text-image pre-training data.
futureDirections.quote: We leave a detailed study of how GLIP scales with text-image data size to future work.

futureDirections.direction: Design better prompts using more expressive class descriptions or the preferences of the pre-trained language model.
futureDirections.quote: One could design better prompts, by providing more expressive descriptions of these classes and/or by exploiting the preference of a pre-trained language model.

futureDirections.direction: Scale up grounding data as a promising alternative to scaling up human-annotated detection data.
futureDirections.quote: We conclude that grounding data are indeed more semantic-rich and a promising alternative to scaling up detection data.

deploymentClaims: One centralized GLIP model can serve various downstream tasks, reducing fine-tuning and deployment cost.
Prompt tuning almost matches full-model tuning without changing any grounding-model parameters.
Language-aware deep fusion adds less than 1x computational cost (Table 7).

evidence.quote: This greatly reduces deployment cost because it allows one centralized model to serve various downstream tasks
By only tuning the prompt embeddings, GLIP-T and GLIP-L can achieve performance close to full-model tuning, allowing for efficient deployment.
Table 7 shows that the language-aware deep fusion brings less than 1x additional computational cost overall.
